prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, opening the regime of 10^-18 fractional uncertainty in time and frequency measurement

statement.case_for: I am withdrawing the second part of my round-1 configuration and now propose B035 alone. The optical lattice clock is a single, sharply defined achievement: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removes the light-shift problem so that a large ensemble of neutral atoms can be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime and interrogated in parallel, and Ye's group carried that scheme to the 10^-18 regime and showed that many-body and systematic effects can be controlled. The result is reproduced and compared by several independent laboratories, it already feeds tests of the constancy of fundamental constants, searches for new physics and relativistic geodesy, and the discussion on redefining the second gives timeliness without the prize depending on that decision. All eight members proposed exactly Katori and Ye, seven prefer B035, and the reasons offered are scientific and have survived the round-1 cross-examination. On the chair's first question, I find the distinction from 2005 and 2012 real: the comb is the counting mechanism and the 2012 prize concerned control of single ions, whereas the lattice clock is a different scheme in which a magic wavelength decouples the clock transition from the trap, giving many-atom interrogation. The citation should name the invention and realization, with the 10^-18 regime as the demonstrated consequence.
statement.case_against: The reservation that every supporter shares still stands: lattice clocks may be read as an excellent refinement of a line honoured in 2005 and 2012, and Lemonde, Takamoto and the Sr and Yb groups at SYRTE, PTB and NIST made material contributions that a two-name prize leaves out. Ye's credit is also partly a continuation of the programme recognised in 2005, so the citation must be tied to the lattice clock and not to precision spectroscopy in general. The redefinition of the second has not happened. Finally, a one-part prize with a free third place can look thin, but I have no second achievement that I can defend with a clean attribution. My own proposal of IceCube credited to Halzen alone does not meet that test, because it omits Karle and Spiering, whom the ballot names, and no colleague has accepted a one-name credit as a fair representation of the discovery.

responses.point: Lindroth reads the IceCube case as weaker than the clock on the unsettled origin of the flux and on attribution, and keeps B023 as a runner-up for a later year.
responses.response: I now agree with you on both counts and have dropped B023 from my configuration. The diffuse flux is established, but a prize usually rests on a result whose meaning is settled, and the source picture (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) is still partial. On attribution, my own one-name Halzen credit and your Halzen-Karle pair both depend on a judgement about AMANDA-era leadership that the supplied material does not resolve. You were also right that we are close on the merit of the clock itself, and I no longer need a second part to justify the configuration.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube below the other candidates because the origin of most of the flux is unresolved and water-based confirmation is incomplete, and calls a three-name collaboration prize an arbitrary selection.
responses.response: You have persuaded me. A prize that squeezes a collaboration-scale discovery into whatever places remain after the clock pair is an arbitrary selection, and the better time for it is once source identification and independent KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD confirmation are firmer. I also take your point about novelty on the clock side, which I answer by having the citation name the invention and the magic-wavelength scheme specifically, as Mehlig proposed. I would want that wording recorded, since it is what separates this prize from a sequel to 2005 and 2012.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B008 for its new organizing principle and rapid decisive experiment, but says he would not defend it against a well-argued shift to B035 because of the credit problem, and doubts whether the 2016 prize leaves room for Z2 insulators.
responses.response: I take the conceptual argument for B008 seriously and have kept it as my first alternative. Where we agree is that the attribution is the obstacle: the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal made Molenkamp's measurement possible, Zhang is deceased, and the three-dimensional generalisation lies outside the three names. Your remark that you would not defend B008 against a well-argued case for B035 is the honest position, and I think the B035 case is now argued. If the committee could settle the HgTe credit in a principled way, B008 would deserve a prize of its own, and I would not call it overlapping with 2016, but I do not think we can settle it this year.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that B008 may be the more far-reaching science but that a clean attribution should not count for more than the science, and proposes drafting the B035 citation around the specific many-atom magic-wavelength invention.
responses.response: I accept your drafting suggestion and use it in my citation, while keeping the 10^-18 regime as the demonstrated consequence. I agree that clean attribution is not a measure of merit, and I do not rest on it: for the clock the science is mature, independently reproduced and consequential. I disagree with only one point of emphasis. A cleaner credit is more than a convenience, because a prize that rewards the right two people is itself a scientific judgement, and in B008 that judgement is exactly the one we cannot make with three names.

responses.point: Kroll separates the IceCube discovery from source identification, notes that Halzen, Karle and Spiering are hard to separate from AMANDA and Baikal contributors, and says metrology has not been over-rewarded since neutral-atom lattice clocks are not covered by 2005 or 2012.
responses.response: Your separation of the diffuse-flux discovery from source identification is correct, and together with the attribution problem it is why I have withdrawn B023. On the novelty question we now agree, and your point that independent laboratories reproduced the 10^-18 performance, a stricter test than many ideas have faced, supports the maturity argument. Your Boulder connection to the comb environment deserves the note you gave it, but it does not touch Katori or Ye personally and I see no need for you to recuse.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the magic-wavelength lattice with many-atom interrogation is a distinct invention and not a continuation of the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.

Whether a two-name credit for Katori and Ye adequately reflects the contributions of Lemonde, Takamoto and the other Sr and Yb clock groups, or whether this is only a limitation to be noted in the record.
How the pending redefinition of the second should be weighed; I treat it as supporting rather than necessary.
I rely on my general knowledge of the clock timeline and have not verified every priority detail beyond the material supplied.
statement.conflict_note: I have documented professional connections to the Fermi-LAT and PAMELA collaborations and work in astroparticle physics at KTH. My round-1 configuration contained IceCube (B023), where I flagged Fermi-LAT follow-up of TXS 0506+056 as a proximity issue; I have withdrawn that part, so the issue no longer bears on my preferred configuration. I have no recorded tie to Katori, Ye or any other credited candidate on the shortlist, and I do not request a recusal on B035.
